_areas_note: ONLY Little Tahoma is listed, deliberately. Pinnacle Peak and The Castle were checked and dropped from `areas`: both are a four-mile round trip with about 1,700 feet of gain from the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road, done in a half day by nearly everyone, and the existing Tatoosh zone already carries every camp that serves them — Snow Lake, the cross-country zone under Unicorn and The Castle, the Reflection Lakes winter snow camp, the Paradise winter group area, Cougar Rock and Ohanapecosh. There is genuinely nothing to add for them, and padding this file with a second copy of those six sites would be worse than leaving them out. Little Tahoma is served by the Fryingpan Creek trailhead on White River Road, a few miles inside the White River entrance, for the Fryingpan and Whitman Glacier route and the East Shoulder. Its Cowlitz and Ingraham Glacier South Face variant is not a Summerland climb at all — it stages from Camp Muir out of Paradise, which the Mount Rainier zone already covers, so Camp Muir is not repeated here. White River Campground and Cougar Rock are likewise already in that zone and are not duplicated.

sites.name: Summerland Camp
sites.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet
sites.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
sites.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
sites.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.

sites.name: Meany Crest
sites.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities
sites.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
sites.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
sites.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.

sites.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
sites.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes
sites.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
sites.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
sites.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.

sites.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
sites.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed
sites.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
sites.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
sites.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.

sites.name: Silver Springs Campground
sites.capacity: Around 55 individual drive-in sites plus one group site taking roughly 20 to 50 people; tents and RVs, no hookups
sites.water: Drinking water on site during the operating season, with flush and vault toilets. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site
sites.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed Forest Service campground outside the park boundary, reservable through the federal booking system. It sits outside the national park, which means it is not subject to the park entrance fee or to any timed-entry reservation the park may be operating for its corridors; you pay and queue for those the following morning on the way in. This covers the campground only, and has nothing to do with either the wilderness permit or the climbing fee, both of which you still need.
sites.notes: The practical roadhead base for a Little Tahoma trip, on the White River about a mile outside the park's White River entrance and a short drive from the Fryingpan Creek trailhead. Its usefulness is timing: the park's own drive-in campground on this side is the highest in the park and normally the last to open, typically not until late June, so for an early-season attempt on Little Tahoma this is often the nearest bed available. It is low, forested and comfortable, with real water and real toilets, and worth nothing at all for acclimatisation. Book it if you want an unhurried night before the approach without spending a wilderness permit on it.
